data.description: RiotPlan needs a remote HTTP MCP server (like Protokoll) instead of running as a local MCP. Plans should be stored centrally as a service, not scattered across project directories. This would eliminate the need to specify plan directories and allow working across workspaces with a single plan database.

data.content: That's what I'm starting to realize I'm starting to realize that RiotPlan probably needs to have a remote HTTP server in the same way that the Protokoll project does. What I'm gonna need to do is start up a remote HTTP server that has a plan directory and then have a way for that MCP server to allow you to create and rate execute the transition plans remotely. I don't think RiotPlan is going to be something that you run as a local MCP. The only reason I'm saying that right now is because I think there's more that we can do if it's remote, and if the contents of the plan are stored separate from the projects themselves. I'm also starting to realize like I don't wanna have to deal with telling it where the directory is. I don't wanna have to deal with having a separate directory everywhere I'm working. I really just want plans to be something that's like a service in the same way that Protokoll does transcriptions. So if I'm working across workspaces, I just have a database that I can hit that has plans.
data.context: User explaining the initial vision and motivation for remote HTTP MCP
data.speaker: user

data.note: Core insight: RiotPlan should follow the Protokoll architecture pattern - a remote HTTP server that MCP clients connect to, rather than running as a local MCP server embedded in each workspace.
Pain point: Currently have to specify plan directories everywhere. Don't want to manage separate plan directories in each workspace. Want plans to "just work" across all workspaces.
Plans as a service: Like Protokoll handles transcriptions centrally, RiotPlan should handle plans centrally. One database/service that all workspaces connect to.

data.content: I think the friction I'm hitting is like every time I have to create a plan, I have to create a new directory and that's to say in this directory, I'd like to explore a plan. I really would just like to get to the point where my local workspace doesn't know about where the plan is other than it's a remote service that I call that creates and stores plans. Also, when I'm going to be crafting agents to run plan steps, I just want them to connect to something else. I don't want them to have a file system in which there's a plan that they can go look at. Plan sharing is impossible unless you just copy that stuff around with files. I don't want to do that. And I just really, I just think that cross workspace will be easier if I myself have a plan service directory running. That's a remote service. It's also more isolation between the LLMs and the plans.
data.context: User explaining friction points and benefits of remote architecture
data.speaker: user

data.note: Friction: Every plan requires creating a directory and specifying "in this directory, explore a plan." Want the workspace to be unaware of plan storage location.
Agent isolation: When crafting agents to run plan steps, they should connect to a service, not have filesystem access to plan files. This provides isolation between LLMs and plans.
Plan sharing is currently impossible without copying files around. A remote service would make sharing trivial.

data.constraint: Local workspace should not know where plans are stored - only that there's a remote service to call
Agents executing plan steps should not have filesystem access to plan files - they connect to a service

Primary usage model shift: RiotPlan's primary interface will be remote MCP server, not local MCP server. This is a fundamental change in how RiotPlan is consumed.

data.name: Layered Integration
data.description: Integrate riotplan-format into the existing riotplan package first, wiring the StorageProvider into existing tools and operations. Then add the HTTP server as a new transport alongside stdio — both transports share the same tool implementations. VSCode extension built last against the running server. Migration is a separate CLI command using riotplan-format's PlanMigrator. This preserves the existing tool logic and adds HTTP as another way to access it.
tradeoffs: Pro: Existing ~40 tools work with both stdio and HTTP transports automatically
Pro: Single codebase for plan operations — no duplication
Pro: riotplan-format integration benefits the local MCP too
Con: Slower to get HTTP server running — lots of integration work upfront
Con: Carries legacy tool complexity into the HTTP API (contradicts 'simplify the API' goal)
Con: StorageProvider integration touches many files in riotplan
assumptions: Existing tool implementations can be adapted to work through StorageProvider without major rewrites
The simplified HTTP API can be achieved by selectively exposing tools rather than rewriting them

data.name: Standalone HTTP Server
data.description: Build the HTTP server as a fresh entry point that uses riotplan-format's StorageProvider directly — not through the existing riotplan tool layer. Design a curated, simplified set of MCP tools from scratch that call the StorageProvider API. The server is a new src/mcp/server-hono.ts in the riotplan repo but with its own tool definitions. VSCode extension built against this clean API. Migration is a separate one-time script. The local stdio MCP continues using the old file-based approach unchanged.
tradeoffs: Pro: Clean break — design the API you actually want without legacy baggage
Pro: Directly aligns with 'simplify and reshape the API' goal
Pro: Faster to prototype — StorageProvider API maps cleanly to tools
Pro: HTTP server and local MCP evolve independently
Con: Two codepaths for plan operations (local tools vs HTTP tools)
Con: Bug fixes or features may need implementing in both places
Con: Local MCP doesn't benefit from riotplan-format integration
assumptions: The simplified HTTP tool set is meaningfully different enough from the local tools to justify separate implementations
Divergence between local and HTTP codepaths is acceptable in the medium term

data.name: Server-Driven Migration
data.description: Build the HTTP server so it can read both directory-based plans AND .plan files. On startup, point it at the source directories (kjerneverk/plans, redaksjon/plans, etc.) and it automatically discovers and migrates plans to .plan format in the unified directory. The server IS the migration tool — no separate step. Uses riotplan-format's StorageProvider for .plan files and a lightweight directory reader for legacy plans. Once all plans are migrated, the directory reading code becomes dead. Fresh simplified MCP tools, like the Standalone approach.
tradeoffs: Pro: No separate migration step — server handles it
Pro: Immediate value — start the server and everything just works
Pro: Graceful transition — plans migrate as they're accessed or on first startup
Con: Server is more complex — understands two formats during transition
Con: Directory reading code is throwaway after migration completes
Con: Migration edge cases could cause data issues if not carefully handled
Con: Harder to test — two code paths that produce the same output
assumptions: Migration is a one-time event, not an ongoing need
Directory-based plans can be reliably converted without data loss
The complexity of dual-format support is justified by the convenience

data.feedback: User leaning toward Standalone HTTP Server but wants clarity on two things before committing: (1) What does migration look like concretely? (2) How does this affect day-to-day usage — what changes for the user?

User reconsidering earlier decision to keep local MCP. The standalone approach creates a natural tension: if the HTTP server is the primary interface and plans live centrally, what's the local MCP for? Maybe cleaner to go all-in on remote and drop local MCP entirely.

Final decision: Go with Standalone HTTP Server. Preserve local MCP server to avoid disruption. Gradually migrate to the new model over time. This is a pragmatic choice — build the new thing, don't break the old thing, let adoption happen naturally.

data.reason: Clean break from legacy tool complexity. Lets us design the simplified API from scratch against riotplan-format's StorageProvider. Local MCP preserved to avoid disruption — gradual migration over time. HTTP server becomes the primary interface for MCP clients and VSCode extension, while CLI can use StorageProvider directly if needed.
